title: Gulab jamun
subtitle: deep-fried milk-solid dumplings in rose syrup
excerpt: Gulab jamun are small, golden-brown dumplings made from dried milk solids, fried until spongy, then soaked in a fragrant rose-and-cardamom sugar syrup. They absorb the syrup as they rest, swelling slightly and taking on a sweet, perfumed quality that deepens overnight. Serve warm with a scoop of kulfi or plain at room temperature.
sourceNotes: Gulab jamun are a staple of the South Asian subcontinent and diaspora, appearing across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. The name comes from the Persian and Urdu words for rose (gulab) and plum (jamun), reflecting the syrup's fragrance and the dumpling's colour. Recipes built on khoya (dried milk solids) appear in Mughal-era culinary records and remain unchanged in form, though the modern shortcut of milk powder has become standard. The fried-then-soaked technique is common to several Middle Eastern and Central Asian sweets of the same period.

recipe.batchNotes: The dumplings keep in the syrup, refrigerated, for up to five days. The flavour improves after the first 24 hours.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before serving; overnight soaking produces fuller-flavoured dumplings.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: frying oil, 170–180°C; lower temperatures leave the centre raw, higher temperatures burn the outside before the inside cooks through

content.text: Gulab jamun are small, golden dumplings fried from dried milk solids and soaked in rose-scented syrup. They come out spongy and syrup-laden, warm and perfumed. The milk-powder dough is forgiving; the main risk is frying too hot, which browns the outside while the centre stays raw.

Combine the sugar and water in a medium saucepan. Bring to the boil, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Add the cardamom pods and simmer for 3 minutes until slightly thickened. Remove from the heat, stir in the rose water, and set aside to keep warm. The syrup wants to be warm when the dumplings go in, hot syrup cracks the skin, cold syrup won't soak through.

Combine the milk powder, plain flour, and baking powder in a medium bowl. Add the ghee and rub it through the powder with your fingertips until evenly distributed. Pour in the milk gradually, stirring with a fork between each addition; you may not need all of it. The dough should come together into a soft, slightly sticky ball that holds its shape without cracking at the edges. If it's too dry and cracking, add milk a teaspoon at a time. Rest the dough for 5 minutes under a clean cloth.

Divide the dough into 20 equal pieces, about 12 g each. Roll each piece between lightly greased palms into a smooth ball with no cracks. A crack will open up during frying and let oil into the centre. If a ball cracks as you roll it, press the dough back together and re-roll.

Heat the oil in a deep medium saucepan to 175°C on a probe thermometer. If hot syrup touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes. Lower 4 to 5 dumplings into the oil at a time; don't crowd the pan or the temperature drops too far. Fry for 6 to 8 minutes, turning gently with a slotted spoon every 90 seconds or so. They should turn a deep mahogany brown all over, darkening evenly. If they colour in under 3 minutes, the oil is too hot, remove the pan from the heat for 30 seconds and check the temperature before continuing.

Lift the fried dumplings directly into the warm syrup with a slotted spoon. Leave them undisturbed for at least 1 hour before serving; the dumplings absorb the syrup and swell slightly. They are ready when they feel soft all the way through when pressed gently with a finger, no resistance at the centre. Serve warm, with a little of the syrup spooned over.
Refrigerate any left over in the syrup. The flavour improves overnight.
